title: National Income and Macroeconomics
lines: Macroeconomics looks at the economy as a whole. USAT questions here are mostly definitions (GDP, GNP, inflation types, unemployment types) plus quick sums with the national income identities, MPC and the multiplier. Learn the chain from GDP to disposable income and the multiplier formula by heart.
## National income accounting
GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year. Only final goods are counted, or the value added at each stage, to avoid double counting.
| Measure | How to get it
| GNP | GDP + net factor income from abroad
| NNP at market price | GNP − depreciation
| National income (NNP at factor cost) | NNP at market price − indirect taxes + subsidies
| Personal income | national income − undistributed profits and company tax − social security contributions + transfer payments
| Disposable income | personal income − personal direct taxes
- Three methods: output (value added), income (wages + rent + interest + profit) and expenditure, C + I + G + (X − M).
- Not counted: transfer payments (pensions, gifts, scholarships), second-hand sales, purely financial deals, unpaid household work.
- Real GDP is valued at base-year prices. Real GDP = nominal GDP × 100 ÷ GDP deflator.
- Per capita income = national income ÷ population.
> GDP = Rs 900 billion. Residents earn Rs 60 billion abroad; foreigners earn Rs 20 billion here.
> Net factor income from abroad = 60 − 20 = 40.
> GNP = 900 + 40 = Rs 940 billion.
! Wheat Rs 500, flour Rs 800, bread Rs 1,200: value added is Rs 1,200, not the Rs 2,500 sum of all sales.
## Consumption and saving
Keynes's psychological law: when income rises, consumption rises but by less. Every extra rupee is spent or saved.
- APC = C ÷ Y and APS = S ÷ Y; APC + APS = 1.
- MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY and MPS = ΔS ÷ ΔY; MPC + MPS = 1.
- For C = a + bY, b is the MPC. Saving is zero at the break-even income where C = Y, that is Y = a ÷ (1 − b).
- Paradox of thrift: if everyone tries to save more, income falls and total saving may not rise.
## Investment and the multiplier

Investment means spending on new capital goods, not buying existing shares or gold. Keynes: firms invest while the marginal efficiency of capital (expected return) exceeds the rate of interest. Autonomous investment does not depend on income; induced investment does. The accelerator says investment depends on the rate of change of output.
Multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ MPS, and ΔY = k × ΔI (or ΔG).
> MPC = 0.75 and investment rises by Rs 20 billion.
> ΔY = 4 × 20 = Rs 80 billion.
! 1 ÷ MPC (1.33 here) is the classic wrong answer. Always divide by the MPS.
- Higher MPC gives a bigger multiplier; saving, taxes and imports are leakages that shrink it.
- Balanced budget multiplier = 1: equal rises in G and taxes raise income by the amount of G.
- Equilibrium in a two-sector model: planned saving = planned investment.
## Employment and unemployment

Classical economists relied on Say's law, 'supply creates its own demand', and flexible wages, so lasting unemployment was impossible. Keynes argued employment depends on effective demand, so unemployment can persist.
| Type | Cause
| Frictional | moving between jobs, searching
| Structural | change in technology or demand makes skills obsolete
| Cyclical | fall in aggregate demand in a recession
| Seasonal | work only in certain seasons (sugar mills, harvest)
| Disguised | more people on a job than needed; MP of extra workers is zero
## Inflation
Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, so the value of money falls. Deflation is a sustained fall; disinflation is a slower rate of inflation.
- Demand-pull: too much money chasing too few goods. Cost-push: rising costs such as oil or wages.
- Stagflation: inflation with high unemployment and slow growth. Hyperinflation: extremely rapid price rises.
- Losers: fixed-income earners, savers and lenders. Gainers: borrowers and holders of real goods.
- Inflation rate = (new index − old index) ÷ old index × 100.
> CPI rises from 160 to 176.
## Business cycles
Four phases repeat: recovery, boom (peak), recession, depression (trough). In a recession output falls, unemployment rises and profits fall.
## Fiscal policy

Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxes. Expansionary policy (more spending, lower taxes) fights recession; contractionary policy fights inflation. A budget deficit means spending exceeds revenue. Crowding out: government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment. Automatic stabilisers, such as progressive taxes and unemployment benefits, damp swings without new decisions.
! Fiscal policy belongs to the government's budget; interest rates and money supply belong to monetary policy and the central bank.
## Quick check
- GDP → GNP: add net factor income from abroad. GNP → NNP: subtract depreciation.
- MPC + MPS = 1; k = 1 ÷ MPS.
- Transfer payments are not part of GDP.
- Disguised unemployment: marginal product zero.
